outcomes.text: 2. How can I find out about food?

explainers.title: Getting started: our food chant
explainers.body: Look at a picture of a farm or a market with your grown-up. What can you see? What are the people doing? Then read this chant out loud together. Clap along, and join in on the last line!

explainers.title: 1. The food journey
explainers.body:
Food goes on a journey to get to us. It starts on a farm and ends on our plate. Read the steps with your grown-up. Put them in order, from 1 to 5. Write the number in the box.

Now fill in the missing words. Use these words: grow, packed, truck, market, eat.
bullets: First, the bananas ________ on the farm.
Next they go on a big ________.
Then they are sold at the ________.

rows: The bananas grow on the farm.
The bananas are packed into boxes.
The bananas go on a big truck.
The bananas are sold at the market.
We eat the bananas at home.

explainers.title: 2. How can I find out about food?
explainers.body: If you want to know about food, there are four ways to find out. Read each one. Tick the ways you could try.
bullets: ☐ Talk to people. You could ask a cook or a farmer.
☐ Look for yourself. Look at the food and the packet.

explainers.title: 3. Reading the label
explainers.body:
Lots of food comes in a packet or a bag. The packet has a label. The label can tell us which country the food came from! Look at these labels with your grown-up. Find the country. Is it near or far?

Some food does not come from far away at all. Bananas, sesame and camel milk grow near us, on farms close to home. They do not travel far.

explainers.title: 4. Where in the world?
explainers.body:
Some food grows near us. Some food comes from far away. Draw your own food map with your grown-up. First, put a dot on your home in Hargeisa. Then draw two rings around your home. The first ring is quite far. The second ring is very far.

Now colour where these three foods come from. Use a different colour for each one. Then say if it is near, quite far, or very far.

Which food travelled the shortest way? Which food travelled the longest way? Tell your grown-up.

headers: My food map (mark home, then draw two rings)
rows: Near, quite far, or very far?

explainers.title: 5. What do you think?
explainers.body:
People think different things about food. Some like food from far away. Some like food from near home. Both are okay! Read what each person says. Draw a happy face if they like food from far away. Draw a different face if they like food from near home.

Now say what you think. Use these words: I like food from ... because ... There is no wrong answer.

headers: Far or near? Draw a face
rows: I love to taste dates and rice from far away.
I like our bananas best. They are fresh from a farm near us.
Food from far away gives us more to choose from.
I like to buy from our own farmers. It helps them.

explainers.title: 6. Questions for a food visitor
explainers.body:
Maybe someone who works with food can visit you, like a farmer, a cook, or a market seller. What would you ask them? Think of two questions with your grown-up. Here are some ideas to help:

Write or draw your two questions here.
bullets: What food do you grow or cook?
Where does your food come from?
Do you like food from near or from far?

headers: My questions for our food visitor

explainers.title: 7. Start planning our display
explainers.body:
Soon your group will make a big display about a meal and where its food comes from. Start to think about it now. Pick a simple meal with about three or four foods in it. Hodan's group picked rice and banana.

Tell your group what you already know about the food. Listen to their ideas too. You will make the display together on the next sheet!

explainers.title: Before you go
explainers.body:
You found out so much about food today! Answer these out loud with your grown-up.

Well done! Now turn to the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet to make your very own food display.
bullets: Where does one food you like come from?
Is it from near, or from far?
What is one way to find out about food?

sections.title: Before you begin
sections.body:
Hello, and welcome to your child's Global Perspectives project at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up who will run the unit with your child. Six- and seven-year-olds are early readers, so you will read most of it aloud, look at the pictures together, and do lots of talking. Underneath all that fun, your child is quietly growing big skills: finding things out, comparing, saying what they think, showing and telling, working with others, and looking back at their learning.

This project grows those skills through a topic every child already loves: food. Your child eats food every day, so this is the perfect place to begin. Together you will follow the journey of food from a farm all the way to your plate.

You do not need to be a teacher, and you do not need anything special. You need a warm voice, a little time about twice a week, some paper and crayons, and a few empty food packets from your kitchen. That is how these skills grow.

sections.title: About this project: Where does food come from?
sections.body:
Over this unit, you and your child will explore one big, tasty question: where does food come from? Your child will follow a food's journey from the farm to the market to the plate, learn how to find out about food, discover which foods come from near us and which travel from far away, hear what different people think, and then, best of all, make a group display about a meal and the journey of its ingredients.

The journey is broken into six short, picture-led lessons (1.1 to 1.6), then the group display, then a gentle looking-back. The topic is the fun part; the real learning is happening quietly underneath it.

sections.title: The skills your child will gently grow
sections.body:
This project grows several Global Perspectives skills. Here they are in plain words, with what to listen for:

You will not test these skills or give any marks. You simply give your child lots of friendly chances to practise them, and you notice out loud when they do them well. A warm 'That was great finding out, Hodan' teaches more than any worksheet.
items: Finding out (research) — asking, looking, reading, and looking online with you. Listen for: 'Where does this come from?'
Comparing and sorting (a little analysis) — reading a simple map and seeing which food came from near and which from far. Listen for: 'This one came a long way!'
Saying what I think (opinion) — telling what they think about food from near and far, and why. Listen for: 'I think ... because ...'
Showing and telling (communication) — making a clear display and telling others about it. Listen for: 'Let me show you ...'
Working together (collaboration) — sharing the jobs in a group, taking turns, and helping each other.
Thinking about our learning (reflection) — looking back at what was easy, what was harder, and what helped.

sections.title: The learning goals, in child-friendly words
sections.body: Here are the little goals for this unit. They are written the way we say them to children. There are no codes to remember.
items: I can say how I find out about food.
I can show what I have found out.
I can find out how far my food has travelled.
I can say what I think, and why.
I can help my group make a display about how food gets to our plate.
I can tell other children about our display, and ask and answer questions.
I can talk about what I learned, and what helped me.

sections.title: How this unit works at Ehel Academy
sections.body:
Children of this age are still early readers, so this unit is led by you, the teacher or parent. Ehel Academy's young model has three parts that work together:

There is no rush and no fixed timetable. Spread the six lessons across two or three weeks, or longer. If your child wants to draw the food journey five times, wonderful. Curiosity is the whole point.
items: You, the grown-up, leading the way. You read the pages and the food chant aloud, run the simple activities, and keep it all warm and playful. Each lesson is short, about 20 to 30 minutes, and you can split it into smaller pieces.
Teacher sessions about twice a week. In these live sessions, children share their food maps and displays, and hear other children too. The group display works best with a few children together.

A 24-hour AI tutor, always used with a grown-up. The tutor can read a page aloud, ask your child a friendly question, help look up where a food grows, or be a pretend audience while your child practises the presentation. At this age the tutor is always used with you beside your child, never alone.

sections.title: Meet Hodan and her friends
sections.body:
So the lessons feel friendly, we follow a little girl called Hodan. She goes to Ehel Academy in Hargeisa, and she loves to find out where things come from. Your child can imagine working right alongside her and her friends.

Together they are a little food team. As your child meets each new idea, they will see what Hodan's team does with it. Later, your child will do the very same thing with their own team, which can be classmates, brothers and sisters, or friends.
items: Hodan loves food and loves to ask questions. She always wants to know where things come from.
Bilal likes maps and finding places. He is good at pointing to countries.
Sagal is kind and careful. She is good at listening and remembering the plan.
Ayaan has lots of ideas and loves to draw.
Layla likes talking to people and asking them questions.
Omar likes to help and to share the jobs fairly.

sections.title: How to read the picture pages and the food chant aloud
sections.body: Each lesson begins with a picture and lots of talking. The Activity Sheet also has a short food chant to enjoy together. Here is how to make the most of them:
items: Look first. Point to things in a food picture and name them together: the farm, the workers, the crates, the truck, the market.
Ask gentle questions. 'What are the people doing? What food can you see? Where do you think it is going?'
Read the chant slowly, with a beat. Clap along as you read. Let your child join in on the last line, then read it again faster for a giggle.
Say the food words warmly. Many will be familiar: banana, mango, dates, sesame, sorghum, rice, camel milk, anjero, bariis. Enjoy the sounds.
Let your child talk more than you. A picture is a doorway to talking. Follow where your child leads.

sections.title: How to run the six short lessons
sections.body: Each lesson has the same simple shape: a short Aim (what it is for, just for you), a Talk about part (to get your child thinking and speaking), and a Do part (the hands-on activity). Read the Aim to yourself, then enjoy the Talk about and Do parts together. Lots of talking is exactly right.

sections.title: Lesson 1.1 - Where does our food come from?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child learns that food goes on a journey from the farm to our plate, and meets ways to find out about food.

Talk about. Hold up a food your child likes, such as a banana. Ask: 'Where do you think this came from? How did it get to us?' Let them guess. Every guess is welcome.

Do. Follow the journey of the food from farm to plate. Read the little steps and put them in order together: the food grows on a farm, it is packed into boxes, it goes on a big truck, it is sold at the market, and we eat it at home. Then meet the people who help it along the way:

sections.title: Lesson 1.2 - How far does our food travel?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child sees that some food comes from near and some from far, and reads a simple world map.

Talk about. Ask: 'Which foods do you think grow near us? Which come from far away?' Bananas and sesame grow near us; rice and dates come from far away.

Do. Use the simple world map in the Activity Sheet. Mark your home in Hargeisa with a dot. Draw two rings around it: the first ring is quite far, the second ring is very far. Then colour where three foods come from: a banana from a farm near us (near), dates from Saudi Arabia (quite far), and rice from India (very far). Finish by asking which food travelled the shortest way, and which the longest.

Here the banana is nearest, and the rice is furthest. The rice comes a very long way: it travels by big ship across the sea to the port at Berbera, then by truck up to the market. Some food travels from other towns here in the Horn of Africa, such as Mogadishu, and some comes from far across the sea.

sections.title: Lesson 1.3 - What do people think about our food?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child hears that people think different things about food from near and far, and starts to say what they think and why.

Talk about. Ask: 'Do you like food from our own farms, or food from far away, or both?' Both are fine. There is no wrong answer.

Do. Read a few speech bubbles together. Some people like food from far away because it gives more to taste and more to choose from. Some people like food from near home because it is fresh and it helps our own farmers. Some gently remember that food from very far away travels a long way by ship or plane. Let your child sort them, then say what they think, using 'I think ... because ...'. Keep it balanced and warm; the point is that people can think different things and all be kind.

If you can, plan a small visit from someone who works with food, such as a farmer, a market seller, or a cook. Help your child think of one or two questions to ask them, like 'Where does your food come from?'

sections.title: Lesson 1.4 - Planning our food display
sections.body:
Aim. Your child and their group choose a meal and start to plan a display about the journey of its ingredients.

Talk about. Ask: 'What is a meal you love? What foods are in it?'

Do. With the group, choose a simple meal with about three or four ingredients. Hodan's group chose rice and banana (bariis iyo moos), a Somali favourite. List the ingredients, and for each one talk about where it comes from and how it reaches the plate. Then start a group work plan so everyone has a job. The full steps are in the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet.

sections.title: Lesson 1.5 - Telling others about our display
sections.body:
Aim. Your child tells other children about the display, and asks and answers questions.

Talk about. Ask: 'What will you say first? What do you most want people to know about your food?'

Do. Help the group practise. First rehearse at home with you and, if you like, the AI tutor as a pretend audience. Then present for real to the family or to other children in the teacher session. Use the presentation checklist in the Mini-Project sheet: say the meal, the ingredients, where they come from, how they get to us, how they are grown, and how you use them. Practise asking good questions about the food's journey, and answering them kindly.

sections.title: Lesson 1.6 - What have we learned?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child looks back at the whole project and thinks about their learning and their teamwork.

Talk about. Ask: 'What do you know now that you did not know before? What was easy? What was harder?'

Do. Use the reflection in the Mini-Project sheet. Your child talks about what they know and can do now, a good idea a friend had, how the group helped each other, and what was easy or harder and why. Keep it warm and spoken. This looking-back is a real Global Perspectives skill, and it matters as much as the display.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: These are the words your child will meet in this project. Say them often and warmly. There is no need to test them.

rows: The way food travels from the farm to our plate.
A place where food is grown.
A place where food is sold.
To put food into boxes to keep it safe on its journey.
A big vehicle that carries food along the road.
To learn something by asking, looking or reading.
The little words on a food packet. It can tell you the country.
A big place with a name, like Somalia, India or Italy.
A picture of the world that shows where places are.
Close to us, not far away.
Pictures and words we put up to show what we found out.
One of the foods we use to make a meal.
To stand up and tell others about our work.

sections.title: What you will need
sections.body: Nothing fancy. Gather a few of these before you start, and keep them in a box:
items: Paper and crayons or coloured pencils.
A few empty, clean food packets or labels from the kitchen, such as a rice bag, a pasta packet, or a tin.
One big sheet of paper for the group display.
A simple picture of a world map (there is one in the Activity Sheet, or print one).
The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet from this unit.
A warm voice and a little time, about twice a week.

sections.title: Using the AI tutor together
sections.body:
At this age, the AI tutor is a helper you use side by side with your child, never a babysitter. Sit together, and let the tutor do the things a patient, friendly helper does well:

Whenever you see an Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up) box in your child's sheets, that is your cue to open the tutor together. Keep it short and cheerful, and always stay in the room. If the tutor ever suggests something you would rather not do, simply skip it. You are always in charge.
items: Read aloud. Ask it to read a page, the food chant, or a checklist slowly, so your child can follow.
Ask a friendly question. Ask it to ask your child one question about food, then let your child answer out loud to you.
Help look something up. Ask it where a food grows, then find that country together on the map.
Help practise the presentation. Let the tutor be a friendly pretend audience while your child rehearses the display.

sections.title: The final task: a food display
sections.body: Everything leads to this. In a small team, your child will choose a meal, find out where its ingredients come from, make a display about the journey of the food, and then present it to others. The full, child-friendly steps are in the separate Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Your role is to gather the materials, keep the team kind and fair, and help only when they are truly stuck. A bright, hand-made display that the children are proud of is a complete success.

sections.title: Simple ways to support and extend
sections.body:
Every child is different. Here are gentle ways to make the unit easier, or to add a little more for a child who is ready.

To support a child who finds it tricky:

To extend a child who wants more:
items: Read every part aloud, and let your child point or draw instead of writing.
Do one small piece at a time, and stop while it is still fun.
Use real food from your kitchen. Hold a banana, a bag of rice, and a packet of pasta, and find the country together.
Let your child talk their answer instead of writing it. Talking always counts.
Find one more food at home and hunt for its country on the label.
Count how many foods in your kitchen come from far away.
Draw a longer journey with more pictures, or add a ship and a plane.
Let your child teach you one thing they found out. Teaching is the best way to remember.

sections.title: Keeping it warm and fun
sections.body: You now have everything you need. Go at your child's pace, celebrate every guess and every drawing, and talk far more than you worry about getting it 'right'. If your child finishes this unit knowing that food goes on a journey, that some food is near and some is far, and that they can find out and tell others, then this project has done its job beautifully. Have fun, together.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: This is the big one! At Ehel Academy, Hodan and her friends made a food display together, and now it is your turn. With your group and a grown-up, you will make a display about a meal and the journey of its food. Then you will look back and think about how your team did. Take your time, share the jobs, and be kind to each other.

steps.title: Choose your meal
steps.intro:
Talk together and choose one meal you all like. Pick a simple meal with about three or four foods in it. Here are some ideas:

Hodan's group chose rice and banana. Write or draw your meal here.
items: rice and banana (bariis iyo moos)
anjero with a banana and a cup of shaah (tea)
rice with vegetables
bread and camel milk for breakfast

steps.title: List the foods and where they come from
steps.intro: Write the foods in your meal. For each one, talk about where it comes from. Is it near or far? Here is how Hodan's group did it.

steps.title: Choose your team jobs
steps.intro:
Every person needs a job. Decide together who will do each one. If lots of you want the same job, take turns or have a quick vote. Here is how Hodan's group shared the jobs:

Now make your own work plan. Write each person's name, what they will tell, and what they will show.

rows: where the rice comes from (far, India)
a world map and a ship
where the sesame oil comes from (near)
the sesame seeds and the mill
how we cook and eat the meal

steps.title: Find out what you need to know
steps.intro:
You know some things already. Some things you need to find out. Talk about each food. These question cards can help:

Put what you know and what you need to find out in this table. Then find out the answers by asking people, reading a book, or looking online with a grown-up.
items: Where do people grow it?
How does it travel to us?
Where is it sold?
How do we cook it?

headers: What we need to find out

steps.title: Make your display
steps.intro:
Now make your big display together! On a big sheet of paper, show the journey of your food from the farm to your plate. Draw these pictures:

Add a world map to show where each food comes from. Colour the near foods one colour and the far foods another colour. Add labels and pictures. Make it bright and clear!
items: Draw the farm where the food grows.
Draw the food being packed into boxes.
Draw the truck. Add a big ship too, if the food comes from far.
Draw the market where the food is sold.
Draw your family eating the meal at home.

steps.title: Practise, then present
steps.intro:
Before you show your display to everyone, practise it first. Rehearse at home with your grown-up, and with your AI tutor as a pretend audience. Then present for real to your family, or to other children in the teacher session.

When you present, use this checklist. Tick each one when you have said it.

steps.title: Ask and answer good questions
steps.intro:
When you visit other groups, ask a good question about their food. A good question is about the food's journey. Read these questions. Draw a happy face next to the good food-journey questions.

Now think of one good question of your own to ask another group. Start it with How, Where, Why, or How far.

When someone asks about your display, listen carefully and answer them kindly.

headers: Good food question? Draw a face
rows: Why does the rice travel by ship?
How far does the banana come?

reflection.prompt: How helpful were you to your team today? Colour in a star for every way you helped. Colour as many as you like!
How do you feel about your team's display? Circle one face:
I have learned about these foods: ...
A good idea my friend had was ...
It was easy to find out about ... because ...
It was harder to find out about ... because ...

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.

selfAssessment.statement: Our display shows where our food comes from.
We all had a job, and we did it.
Everyone in our team shared an idea.
We took turns and helped each other.
